title: The Last Flourish
passage:
When the Halberg Savings Bank cleared out its basement last spring, it turned up eleven thousand signature cards, filed since 1908: stiff paper squares on which every new customer had once been made to write his name three times, so that a clerk could later judge whether the signature on a cheque was a ___(1)___ or merely the same hand on a bad day. Marit Solberg, the archivist hired to catalogue them, spent four months among the boxes and came away with a question she had not expected to ask — what, exactly, did the third signature prove?

The bank's own manuals are candid enough. A clerk was not matching shapes but reading habits: the pressure at the turn of a letter, the point where the pen left the paper, the speed that thirty years of practice had made automatic. Copy those and you must slow down; slow down and the line goes even, and it was that evenness, more than any tremor of the hand, that ___(2)___ the imitator. ___(3)___, none of this amounted to a science. Solberg found dozens of disputed cases in the ledgers, several of them settled by nothing better than a manager's memory of a face.

What has replaced the cards is not, as is often assumed, a cruder instrument. A signature written on a screen is judged on stroke order, timing and pressure — measurements the paper card never held — and, on the narrow question of whether two hands are the same hand, it is plainly the better test. Yet Solberg declines to call the change a straightforward ___(4)___. The old arrangement asked someone who knew you to vouch for you; the new one asks nothing of anybody, and when it refuses a match there is no clerk to argue with and no memory of a face to appeal to.

The flourish she expects to survive: a scrawl dragged across a courier's screen with a fingertip, illegible, unexamined, demanded all the same, long after it has stopped ___(5)___ any weight.
— Ellen Ravnsborg, columnist

questions.rationale: Collocation/sense gap on a suffix-rhymed -ery/-ury noun set: three of the four belong to the vocabulary of deception, the fourth (mockery) to that of ridicule. The frame — 'judge whether the signature on a cheque was a ___ or merely the same hand on a bad day' — sets up a two-way choice between a name written by somebody else and a genuine name written badly, so the gap must be the countable noun for a faked signature: 'was a forgery' locks. mockery = sense misfit (grammatical with the article, but it names a travesty or an object of ridicule, not a document written in another person's name; a clerk comparing cards is not judging whether a cheque insults him). perjury = wrong domain plus countability (a false statement made under oath, not a copied hand, and the noun is not used with 'a' in this sense). trickery = countability misfit (an uncountable abstract noun; 'was a trickery' is not English, though the theme of deception makes it the most tempting shape-match). Only 'forgery' is both countable and the exact term the contrast demands.

Particle-discrimination collocation gap: four real phrasal verbs sharing one head verb, so the options are maximally shape-matched and POS-uniform. The frame needs a verb meaning 'revealed, unintentionally': the copyist's line goes too even, 'and it was that evenness, more than any tremor of the hand, that ___ the imitator'. 'Give away' is the fixed idiom for betraying someone's secret identity, so C locks. gave out = collocation_misfit (means distributed, or — of a machine or a body — failed; neither takes 'the imitator' as the thing exposed). gave up = collocation_misfit (means abandoned or surrendered; it does also have a yielding sense that takes an inanimate subject — 'the sea gave up its dead', 'the soil gave up its secrets' — but there the subject is whatever had been holding the thing concealed, and the evenness of a line conceals nothing, it is itself the evidence; read agentively, 'gave up the imitator' would mean he was handed over rather than detected). gave off = collocation_misfit (its object is whatever is emitted — heat, light, a smell, and figuratively a signal or an air of confidence — never the person exposed; a line can give off a signal, but it cannot give off an imitator). Only 'gave away' carries the sense of an involuntary tell that the sentence has been built around.

Connective-logic gap; all four are sentence-initial linking adverbs (connective class matched). Upstream the paragraph has just described a method that works — a copyist is caught by the evenness of his line — and the gapped sentence withdraws the credit ('none of this amounted to a science'), a concession the following sentence then documents with disputed cases settled by a manager's memory. The relation is therefore concessive-contrastive: 'Nevertheless' is the only fit. Consequently = wrong_logic (asserts cause and effect, but the method's success is not the reason it fails to be a science; the sentence contradicts what precedes it rather than following from it). Meanwhile = wrong_logic (temporal 'at the same time', and no second time-frame or parallel scene is in play). Incidentally = wrong_logic (marks a digression, but the claim is the paragraph's verdict and is immediately supported by evidence, not set aside as an aside). Only 'Nevertheless' matches the reversal the sentence performs.

Polarity gap on a suffix-rhymed -ment noun set. The sentence before concedes the new system's superiority ('on the narrow question of whether two hands are the same hand, it is plainly the better test'), and the gapped sentence opens with 'Yet', which can only qualify that concession: she refuses to call the change a straightforward good thing, and the following clause explains what was lost. 'a straightforward improvement' locks. impoverishment = polarity_mirror (the passage's elegiac register pulls a skimmer toward the negative pole, but 'Yet' after a sentence granting that the screen is the better test cannot introduce a refusal to call the change a loss — that would be agreement, not contrast, and would leave the paragraph without an argument). endorsement = surface_word_match (an endorsement is what a signature written on the back of a cheque is called, so the banking context makes the word feel at home, but 'call the change a straightforward endorsement' says she declines to treat the change as an act of approval, which is not what the sentence is doing). entrenchment = collocation_misfit (a digging-in or consolidation of something already established; there is no idiom 'a straightforward entrenchment', and nothing in the passage is being consolidated). Only 'improvement' completes the concession-plus-qualification the 'Yet' demands.

Collocation gap: four -ing participles that all form real English collocations with 'weight', only one of which means what the frame needs. The closing sentence predicts that the signature will still be demanded 'long after it has stopped ___ any weight' — that is, long after it has ceased to count for anything, which is the fixed idiom 'carry weight' (to have force or influence). carrying locks. shifting = collocation_misfit (a real phrase, but 'shift one's weight' describes moving the body's mass from one foot to the other, a physical act a signature cannot perform). gaining = collocation_misfit (a real phrase meaning to grow heavier, and thematically inverted: the sentence is about losing force, not putting on mass). pulling = collocation_misfit (the idiom is 'pull one's weight', meaning to do one's fair share, and it requires the possessive; 'stopped pulling any weight' both breaks the idiom's form and names the wrong quality). Only 'carrying' gives the sense of authority draining away that the whole passage has been arguing toward.

generator_meta.topic: the disappearance of the handwritten signature as evidence — what a bank's old signature cards actually tested, and what screen-captured signing gained and lost
